Ben Ngubane and the Zululand Quarries

By: Joy Summers | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
BEN NGUBANE AND HIS ZULULAND QUERRIES Ben Ngubane has been in the news a lot lately. He has just appeared before a parliamentary enquiry into the SABC where he faced a grilling, and he is also a key

Unique Selling Point:
BEN NGUBANE AND HIS ZULULAND QUERRIES


HUNTREX 305

Huntrex 305 is a company owned by Mr Ben Ngubane and his wife, that by itself is not unusual, but it’s the story of this company, that reveals much about the man installed as Eskom’s chairperson. Court documents reveal that Huntrex has defaulted on paying its loans, Ngubane has called upon his political connection, President Zuma to cover for him, and is now using the mining minister to delay court proceedings. Meanwhile court records reveal that he appears to have fraudulently forged false share certificates to hold onto a company that he hasn’t yet paid for.

BEN NGUBANE BUYS A QARRY AND A SAND MINE

The story begins in 2010 when Brikor, a brick company in Gauteng, ended up in a spot of financial bother. They were overdrawn on their overdraft facility by R30 million. FNB were unimpressed and wanted their money back. If not, they threatened Brikor that they would liquidate them.

Brikor decided to free up some cash to repay FNB, by selling their STANGER operation for R50 million rand. The Stanger operation consisted of a sand mine and a quarry and the mineral rights for that. Enter willing buyers Mr Ben Ngubane and his wife Sheila.

The Ngubane’s bought the entire operation and put it into what was a dormant company called Huntrex 305. Huntrex acquired all the assets of immovable property, the equipment and shares in Zululand quarries PTY LTD and Natal Sands PTY ltd. Presumably, they planned to operate the quarry and sand mining operation as a profitable business. It had a history of making a former rally driver very wealthy. Before Brikor owned the operation, it had been owned by rally driver called Jannie Habig, who had turned over R15 million rand a month and sold the business for R100 million to Brikor.

NO MONEY HONEY

But Ben Ngubane had no money to buy the business, so he approached the KZN provincial bank, Ithala for a loan of R30 million rand. The bank agreed. They funded the balance of R20 million in installments they would pay to Brikor who agreed to the terms, and the deal was sealed.


THE HONEYMOON

Now the Ngubane’s had themselves a quarry and sand mine, but with that came the repayments of the loan so they could call it their own. A million rand every month, R600 000 to Ithala bank and R400 000 to Brikor. For the first six months, they paid a million rand monthly, that they owed. Then after paying back less than 10% of the loan, they just stopped paying.

ITHALA SAYS SHOW ME THE MONEY

By the end of 2013 Ithala bank’s attorneys tell Ben and Sheila, that if they don’t pay up, the bank will liquidate Huntrex. The Ngubane’s responded by fighting back and bought an interdict to stop Ithala bank from liquidating them. In his application Ben Ngubane claimed that he had made a verbal arrangement with the CEO of Ithala bank that the loan wasn’t due and payable and therefore Ithala couldn’t liquidate! Ithala refuted this.

TO COURT AND BACK AGAIN

By Feb 2014 Ithala bank launched a counter application which included asking the court to provisionally liquidate the Ngubane’s company Huntrex. Its opposed. 2014 was spent backwards and forwards in a legal joust, until finally on the 31 March 2015 all the applications were set down to be heard.

THE ESKOM CHAIRMAN, A CONVENIENT EXCUSE, AND AN UNWAVERING JUDGE

Mr Ben Ngubane’s counsel stood up in court and told the judge that Mr Ngubane had been appointed as chairman of Eskom, he was busy with matters of national security and therefore the judge should postpone the matter indefinitely. But that didn’t wash with the judge, who said he didn’t care who the counsel’s client was, and without further ado he granted the provisional liquidation to ITHALA BANK.

A FRONT POPS UP

Four liquidators were appointed to manage Huntrex and keep the quarry going. One of the liquidators is an attorney at Stowell and Co. Attorneys, Mr Neil Button.

“Our job was to preserve the assets” he told Carte Blanche. To ensure the business remained viable both Brikor and Ithala helped with some funding.

The return date to put the company into final liquidation had been set down for August 2015, but the day before they were supposed to return to court, a lady called Janakey Reddy brought an application to put the company in Business rescue. She said she had sufficient funds to make it viable. But it turned out that Ms. Reddy was just the human resources manager at Huntrex ,who earned around R13 000 per month and had no other funding. She had been set up as a front by the NGUBANE’S.

On the 10th December 2015, the court finally heard the two applications. The first was the case for business rescue which was defeated with costs, which is unfortunate for Mrs. Reddy as it meant she had to find the cost of several very expensive senior counsel. Then the liquidators fired her.

MICHAEL HULLEY SWOOPS IN LIKE BEN NGUBANE’S ANGEL

The second application heard on the 10th December was to confirm a date for final liquidation. Then counsel for Ithala bank makes a surprise admission. They tell the court that on the 9th December 2015, the day before they appeared in court, President Zuma’s attorney, Mr Michael Hulley, had arrived at ITHALA, convened a full board meeting of senior executives, and told them that the president had said they must “leave his man alone.” Ithala said no.

Soon after Huntrex was put into final liquidation and Mr Hulley began to play a more prominent role. Mr Ngubanes original lawyer Mr Manogh Maharaj disappears.

THE HOME STRETCH

As per final liquidations, a process unfolds and a first meeting was held with creditors. The debts are discussed and by now they have ballooned to R75 million including interest:
As at December 2015 HUNTREX owes:
R34 million is owed to Ithala Bank
R24 million to Brikor
R1 million to the municipality in unpaid debts
R4 million to the receiver for VAT
R12 million to concurrent creditors

Sandton Plant hire are keen buyers but they want to buy the whole bundle, the quarry, the sand mine, the mineral rights and the shares in Huntrex. But there’s a problem. Even though the shares in Huntrex have no value at that point, Ben Ngubane and Sheila are still shareholders. The liquidators put together a tripartite agreement and Mr Michael Hulley meets on Mr Ben Ngubane’s behalf. Meetings take place over the first six months of 2016 with Mr Hulley meeting the liquidators on behalf of Mr Ngubane who was away first in Brazil, then Nigeria, then the USA. Mr Hulley says in principle, Mr Ngubane will sell his shares.


THE HOME STRETCH HITS A SNAG
On the 15th June 2016 at the second meeting of the creditors it appears they are making progress. The liquidators have it recorded that they have received an offer of R30 million and Sheila Ngubane and her accountant adopts the report and sign the minutes. So far so good. Sandton Plant are ready to buy but then they encounter a problem.




ZULULAND QUERRIES – A NEW SET OF SHARE CERTIFICATES
The liquidators have a set of share certificates. But then suddenly Ben and Sheila produce another set of share certificate copies made out in their personal capacities. Ben Ngubane now refuses to sell his shares to the new buyer.

THE MYSTERY OF ZULULAND QUERRIES
The liquidators have both sets of share certificate and it appears the NGUBANE share certificates have been forged. The numbers are not consecutive as they should be; Zululand Quarries is spelt incorrectly as Zululand Querries, and instead of the shares being R1 each as they are in the originals they are recorded at one cent each. The shares should add up to 100 but instead one of the certificates has an adding mistake and reads 170 shares.

Everyone is dumbstruck. Forging share certificates is a criminal offence under the companies act. Michael Hulley suddenly disappears from the scene and Mr Ngubane’s original lawyer Mr Maharaj enters the fray again. The liquidators ask the court for a declaratory order on the certificates but the Ngubanes oppose the declaratory order.

MINISTER OF MINERAL AFFAIRS – GUPTA LINKED, MOSEBENZE ZWANE TO THE RESCUE.
Currently there is an impasse. When the company was sold to the Ngubane’s the mineral rights changed hands without any problem. Strictly speaking, he should have had to reapply for a mining license due to the change of ownership. That didn’t happen, but now that the liquidators are trying to sell the business, the mining minister has intervened and said the new buyers must reapply for a mining right.

The mining minister was supposed to file his affidavit by Tuesday this week. And that is where our story stands at present. Ngubane may yet hold onto an asset he has barely paid for, using the might of his political connections and the odd allegedly fraudulent share certificate.

Script:


Final Script Ben Ngubane TX Sunday 28th May 2017 2 pm

Commentary One
Another week, another Eskom scandal.

Narend Singh
Resigned, unpaid leave, did not resign, thirty million…

Commentary Two
Brian Molefe’ story has changed from resignation, to early retirement and this week when we thought we had heard it all, and despite overwhelming evidence to the contrary, to unpaid leave.

John Steenhuizen
Brian Molefe was not on maternity leave, he was not on long leave. Brian Molefe had resigned from Eskom

Commentary Three
On Tuesday Minister Brown and the Eskom board, led by chairperson Dr. Ben Ngubane, faced bristling MP’s at a parliamentary meeting to explain why Brian Molefe was back at Eskom.

Up sound Ben Ngubane
We are not re employing this man, he was simply reverting to the status quo because the original agreement that he can take early retirement had been rescinded

Commentary four
But if Eskom has become state capture central, former finance minister Pravin Gordhan has become the symbol of its resistance

Pravin Gordhan
I don’t know whether the board lives in its own oblivion, but the public is connecting the dots, members of the board. They are increasingly aware that you are abusing state property and state resources in the name of yourselves, not in the name of the South African public

Commentary Five
On Tuesday Dr. Ben Ngubane was lambasted. Yet, he contends his integrity is beyond reproach. As chairman of Eskom, it should be, but is it? To try answer that question, we travelled to the Zululand quarry, close to the banks of the Tugela river, to a mine that’s seen better days

LINK at QUARRY
There is a story behind this once thriving business and the man at the centre of it, is well known to us, because he is also the current chairman of Eskom, Dr Ben Ngubane


Commentary Six
Ngubane has been a cabinet minister, a premier, chairman of the SABC, and a business man. In 2011, Ngubane and his wife Sheila, through their company, Huntrex 305, bought a bundle of businesses that included Zululand Quarries, Natal Sand Supplies, and Stanger Brick and tile. Brikor was the seller. Ina McDonald is the Brikor chair.

Devi
Ina, when the Stanger businesses were sold were they viable businesses?
Ina McDonald
Yes, it was a viable business

Commentary seven
Viable because Zululand Quarries and Natal sand Supplies, had mining and mineral rights.

The total cost of the business was R50 million rand. Funded as follows:
R1 million raised by Ben and Sheila Ngubane
R29 million through a loan from Ithala bank and
R20 million to be paid off to Brikor over 6 years

LINK
The mining and mineral rights were considered by Ithala to be the most valuable assets and the bank made certain those rights were ceded to them as security, until Huntrex paid off the loan.

Commentary eight
Ithala bank declined to comment. But details of their agreement are recorded in court documents. To take us through the story we asked John Walker, who Carte Blanche viewers may remember, as the attorney for the liquidators of Aurora

Devi
Let’s look at Ithala
John
I think Ithala acted very responsibly. As a financier that deals with public funds they structured the deal in such a way that they got all the necessary securities, basically they were protected in law right from the beginning

LINK
The deal was that Huntrex would pay off their loans in instalments over 72 months, around a million a month. But after only six sporadic payments, they just stopped paying

John Walker
When you stop paying your financier right from the beginning, almost within the first three months then the chances of you being liquidated is almost 100%





Commentary nine
The documents tell a story of a quarry with no working capital. Maintenance became a problem, the crusher broke, their suppliers refused to grant them credit. Ngubane blamed the management team, people left. In 2013 Ithala sent Huntrex letters threatening liquidation. By 2014 Huntrex was terminally ill.

LINK
The company was hopelessly insolvent, and the court heard how a R50 million company now found itself with R90 million rand’s worth of debt.

Commentary ten
Ithala appeared to bend over backwards to assist Huntrex, but the Ngubanes as the only directors and shareholders, still didn’t cough up the money, and they owe Brikor R24 million with interest.

John Walker
The court said look you are hopelessly insolvent, you are not going to get out of this. I need to put it into the hands of the liquidator, wind it up in the hands of the master who then represents the creditors in ensuring that there is structure in how the assets are dealt with afterwards

Commentary twelve
The story of Huntrex is still unfolding in the Pietermaritzburg high court. Its sensitive, and none of the critical players would talk on camera, including the Ngubane’s and Stowell and Company, the liquidators in the matter. Perhaps it’s not surprising, because on the eve of the final liquidation in December 2015, Ben Ngubane appears to have called in his connections.

Devi Link
Ben Ngubane has been in the news a lot lately, and downplayed how much clout he has as Eskom’s chairman, but he certainly seems to have the presidents ear, because as Huntrex got deeper into trouble, the president attorney, Michael Hulley paid Ithala a visit.

Commentary thirteen
Mr. Hulley’s involvement in the matter has been confirmed by a source.

John Walker
I was not there, but on the papers, it seems Michael Hulley tried to broker some sort of deal to the benefit of Huntrex and tried to defer the liquidation application which ultimately was rejected by the court

Commentary Fourteen
Mr. Hulley has yet to reply to Carte Blanche. But Ithala’s senior counsel Anthonie Troskie, placed the President’s intervention in the matter, on the court record. Johan Ploos Van Amstel was the judge.

Troskie: They were approached last night, they looked at the proposal and the client
Judge Ploos van Amstel: They met with who?
Adv. Troskie: Representative of number one, M’lord
Judge Ploos van Amstel: No, but did they meet with Sandton Mining?
Adv. Troskie: No, they were from the very top approached
Judge Ploos van Amstel: You mean from the person who dismissed the minister of finance?
Adv. Troskie: The very one M’lord.
Judge Ploos van Amstel: That top?
Adv. Troskie: Yes, that top, and they considered it last night again in possession of these papers and said we are going ahead.
Judge Ploos van Amstel: I think I will have to decide it on the papers before me

Commentary Fifteen
Huntrex was put into final liquidation. Its most valuable assets were the mining and mineral rights in Zululand Quarries and Natal Sand Supplies. Then, Sandton Mining a willing buyer, made an offer

Link
But the optimism didn’t last long when the sale hit a snag no one could have predicted.

Commentary Sixteen
The Ngubane’s asserted that they personally owned Zululand Quarries and Natal sand Supplies

LINK
Effectively they had become the owners of the mineral rights, without which this business has little value.

John
That is the biggest asset of this company. If you dispose of those assets then the liquidator has an empty shell left you have Ithala who financed the acquisition of this company with its mining rights, left with nothing

Commentary seventeen
So, who really owns the shares? Huntrex or Ben and Sheila Ngubane? A share register is like a bible, and Brikor dug theirs out of the archive, at our request.

Ina McDonald
This is the Zululand Quarries company register ok, and it basically tells you who the directors are, and who the shareholders are, and you can see here that the shares were transferred to Brikor in 2008 and then transferred to Huntrex in 2011.

John
This is where the matter becomes quite bizarre. What happened here is that Dr Ngubane and his wife produce share certificates as proof that they had at some stage obtained the shareholding in these two businesses from the liquidated company.
Devi
Could that be true?


John
The first temptation of anyone in financial trouble– many people are tempted to divest themselves of those assets to protect those assets and regain those later when the dust has settled. The law doesn’t allow that. The law says that from the time the Liquidation application is launched -the date of the liquidation gets backdated to the time the papers are launched, Which means that any disposal of assets after the liquidation starts is unlawful.
Devi
So let’s look at dates here then?
John
The liquidation dates back to Feb 2014, the share certs produced by B and S date back to July 2014.

Up sound
Are these copies of the originals?
Yes are
I recognize previous financial director had written on this.

Commentary eighteen
Brikor confirmed their authenticity. These are the new certificates that the liquidators allege are fabricated, forged and sham share certificates. Ithala Bank agrees. In this one, Zululand Quarries becomes Zululand Querries. As John Walker points out there are other anomalies

John
In this instance both companies had share capital of shares at par value of R1 each. The new share certificates, are now shares for 1cent each. There are additional things that concern me. If you look at this instance, the fact that the members register does not record this so called transfer of the shares, the fact that the transfer occurred after the deemed date of liquidation which is unlawful anyway, the name of the company is wrong, the par value of the shares is incorrect. If the allegations contained in the liquidators affidavit is correct, this is not one of the most intellectual methods of trying to divest assets that I have ever seen

Commentary nineteen
Privately and publicy, Ben Ngubane is against the ropes. He says that as the matter pertaining to the Zululand Quarries is before a court he is not at liberty to comment.
In November, the court will determine if the Ngubanes Zululand Querry share certificates are fraudulent. Meanwhile Eskom and the board leads, is running out of runway

Pravin Gordhan
In managing governance in South Africa where there are a significant number of people in the bureaucracy and elsewhere and the boards, who are actually taking a view that says I don’t care if you know what I do, I don’t care if you know that public resources are going elsewhere. I don’t care how many reports that the public protector or anybody else provides because I am protected. The question is by whom and at what cost and how will history record your role ultimately.


THE END DURATION 10 36.

PROMO ONE

Chairperson of Eskom, Dr Ben Ngubane contends that his integrity is beyond reproach. This week MP’s grilled him on the Brian Molefe saga

PROMO TWO
In 2011, Dr Ben Ngubane and his wife bought Zululand Quarries through their company Huntrex 305. Court documents reveal that they have been accused of forging share certificates to lift the assets out of their liquidated company.

PROMO THREE
Did the Presidents attorney Michael Hulley, intervene in a matter between Dr Ben Ngubane and Ithala Bank who was owed millions by Ngubane’s company?

John Walker
it seems Michael Hulley tried to broker some sort of deal to the benefit of Huntrex

Sandton Plant are ready to buy but then they encounter a problem. ZULULAND QUERRIES – A NEW SET OF SHARE CERTIFICATES The liquidators have a set of share certificates. But then suddenly Ben and Sheila produce another set of share certificate copies made out in their personal capacities. Ben Ngubane now refuses to sell his shares to the new buyer. THE MYSTERY OF ZULULAND QUERRIES The liquidators have both sets of share certificate and it appears the NGUBANE share certificates have been forged. The numbers are not consecutive as they should be; Zululand Quarries is spelt incorrectly as Zululand Querries, and instead of the shares being R1 each as they are in the originals they are recorded at one cent each. The shares should add up to 100 but instead one of the certificates has an adding mistake and reads 170 shares. Everyone is dumbstruck. Forging share certificates is a criminal offence under the companies act. Michael Hulley suddenly disappears from the scene and Mr Ngubane’s original lawyer Mr Maharaj enters the fray again. The liquidators ask the court for a declaratory order on the certificates but the Ngubanes oppose the declaratory order. MINISTER OF MINERAL AFFAIRS – GUPTA LINKED, MOSEBENZE ZWANE TO THE RESCUE. Currently there is an impasse. When the company was sold to the Ngubane’s the mineral rights changed hands without any problem. Strictly speaking, he should have had to reapply for a mining license due to the change of ownership. That didn’t happen, but now that the liquidators are trying to sell the business, the mining minister has intervened and said the new buyers must reapply for a mining right. The mining minister was supposed to file his affidavit by Tuesday this week. And that is where our story stands at present. Ngubane may yet hold onto an asset he has barely paid for, using the might of his political connections and the odd allegedly fraudulent share certificate. Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 31 May 2017 Script: Final Script Ben Ngubane TX Sunday 28th May 2017 2 pm Commentary One Another week, another Eskom scandal. Narend Singh Resigned, unpaid leave, did not resign, thirty million… Commentary Two Brian Molefe’ story has changed from resignation, to early retirement and this week when we thought we had heard it all, and despite overwhelming evidence to the contrary, to unpaid leave. John Steenhuizen Brian Molefe was not on maternity leave, he was not on long leave. Brian Molefe had resigned from Eskom Commentary Three On Tuesday Minister Brown and the Eskom board, led by chairperson Dr. Ben Ngubane, faced bristling MP’s at a parliamentary meeting to explain why Brian Molefe was back at Eskom. Up sound Ben Ngubane We are not re employing this man, he was simply reverting to the status quo because the original agreement that he can take early retirement had been rescinded Commentary four But if Eskom has become state capture central, former finance minister Pravin Gordhan has become the symbol of its resistance Pravin Gordhan I don’t know whether the board lives in its own oblivion, but the public is connecting the dots, members of the board. They are increasingly aware that you are abusing state property and state resources in the name of yourselves, not in the name of the South African public Commentary Five On Tuesday Dr. Ben Ngubane was lambasted. Yet, he contends his integrity is beyond reproach. As chairman of Eskom, it should be, but is it? To try answer that question, we travelled to the Zululand quarry, close to the banks of the Tugela river, to a mine that’s seen better days LINK at QUARRY There is a story behind this once thriving business and the man at the centre of it, is well known to us, because he is also the current chairman of Eskom, Dr Ben Ngubane Commentary Six Ngubane has been a cabinet minister, a premier, chairman of the SABC, and a business man. In 2011, Ngubane and his wife Sheila, through their company, Huntrex 305, bought a bundle of businesses that included Zululand Quarries, Natal Sand Supplies, and Stanger Brick and tile. Brikor was the seller. Ina McDonald is the Brikor chair. Devi Ina, when the Stanger businesses were sold were they viable businesses? Ina McDonald Yes, it was a viable business Commentary seven Viable because Zululand Quarries and Natal sand Supplies, had mining and mineral rights. The total cost of the business was R50 million rand. Funded as follows: R1 million raised by Ben and Sheila Ngubane R29 million through a loan from Ithala bank and R20 million to be paid off to Brikor over 6 years LINK The mining and mineral rights were considered by Ithala to be the most valuable assets and the bank made certain those rights were ceded to them as security, until Huntrex paid off the loan. Commentary eight Ithala bank declined to comment. But details of their agreement are recorded in court documents. To take us through the story we asked John Walker, who Carte Blanche viewers may remember, as the attorney for the liquidators of Aurora Devi Let’s look at Ithala John I think Ithala acted very responsibly. As a financier that deals with public funds they structured the deal in such a way that they got all the necessary securities, basically they were protected in law right from the beginning LINK The deal was that Huntrex would pay off their loans in instalments over 72 months, around a million a month. But after only six sporadic payments, they just stopped paying John Walker When you stop paying your financier right from the beginning, almost within the first three months then the chances of you being liquidated is almost 100% Commentary nine The documents tell a story of a quarry with no working capital. Maintenance became a problem, the crusher broke, their suppliers refused to grant them credit. Ngubane blamed the management team, people left. In 2013 Ithala sent Huntrex letters threatening liquidation. By 2014 Huntrex was terminally ill. LINK The company was hopelessly insolvent, and the court heard how a R50 million company now found itself with R90 million rand’s worth of debt. Commentary ten Ithala appeared to bend over backwards to assist Huntrex, but the Ngubanes as the only directors and shareholders, still didn’t cough up the money, and they owe Brikor R24 million with interest. John Walker The court said look you are hopelessly insolvent, you are not going to get out of this. I need to put it into the hands of the liquidator, wind it up in the hands of the master who then represents the creditors in ensuring that there is structure in how the assets are dealt with afterwards Commentary twelve The story of Huntrex is still unfolding in the Pietermaritzburg high court. Its sensitive, and none of the critical players would talk on camera, including the Ngubane’s and Stowell and Company, the liquidators in the matter. Perhaps it’s not surprising, because on the eve of the final liquidation in December 2015, Ben Ngubane appears to have called in his connections. Devi Link Ben Ngubane has been in the news a lot lately, and downplayed how much clout he has as Eskom’s chairman, but he certainly seems to have the presidents ear, because as Huntrex got deeper into trouble, the president attorney, Michael Hulley paid Ithala a visit. Commentary thirteen Mr. Hulley’s involvement in the matter has been confirmed by a source. John Walker I was not there, but on the papers, it seems Michael Hulley tried to broker some sort of deal to the benefit of Huntrex and tried to defer the liquidation application which ultimately was rejected by the court Commentary Fourteen Mr. Hulley has yet to reply to Carte Blanche. But Ithala’s senior counsel Anthonie Troskie, placed the President’s intervention in the matter, on the court record. Johan Ploos Van Amstel was the judge. Troskie: They were approached last night, they looked at the proposal and the client Judge Ploos van Amstel: They met with who? Adv. Troskie: Representative of number one, M’lord Judge Ploos van Amstel: No, but did they meet with Sandton Mining? Adv. Troskie: No, they were from the very top approached Judge Ploos van Amstel: You mean from the person who dismissed the minister of finance? Adv. Troskie: The very one M’lord. Judge Ploos van Amstel: That top? Adv. Troskie: Yes, that top, and they considered it last night again in possession of these papers and said we are going ahead. Judge Ploos van Amstel: I think I will have to decide it on the papers before me Commentary Fifteen Huntrex was put into final liquidation. Its most valuable assets were the mining and mineral rights in Zululand Quarries and Natal Sand Supplies. Then, Sandton Mining a willing buyer, made an offer Link But the optimism didn’t last long when the sale hit a snag no one could have predicted. Commentary Sixteen The Ngubane’s asserted that they personally owned Zululand Quarries and Natal sand Supplies LINK Effectively they had become the owners of the mineral rights, without which this business has little value. John That is the biggest asset of this company. If you dispose of those assets then the liquidator has an empty shell left you have Ithala who financed the acquisition of this company with its mining rights, left with nothing Commentary seventeen So, who really owns the shares? Huntrex or Ben and Sheila Ngubane? A share register is like a bible, and Brikor dug theirs out of the archive, at our request. Ina McDonald This is the Zululand Quarries company register ok, and it basically tells you who the directors are, and who the shareholders are, and you can see here that the shares were transferred to Brikor in 2008 and then transferred to Huntrex in 2011. John This is where the matter becomes quite bizarre. What happened here is that Dr Ngubane and his wife produce share certificates as proof that they had at some stage obtained the shareholding in these two businesses from the liquidated company. Devi Could that be true? John The first temptation of anyone in financial trouble– many people are tempted to divest themselves of those assets to protect those assets and regain those later when the dust has settled. The law doesn’t allow that. The law says that from the time the Liquidation application is launched -the date of the liquidation gets backdated to the time the papers are launched, Which means that any disposal of assets after the liquidation starts is unlawful. Devi So let’s look at dates here then? John The liquidation dates back to Feb 2014, the share certs produced by B and S date back to July 2014. Up sound Are these copies of the originals? Yes are I recognize previous financial director had written on this. Commentary eighteen Brikor confirmed their authenticity. These are the new certificates that the liquidators allege are fabricated, forged and sham share certificates. Ithala Bank agrees. In this one, Zululand Quarries becomes Zululand Querries. As John Walker points out there are other anomalies John In this instance both companies had share capital of shares at par value of R1 each. The new share certificates, are now shares for 1cent each. There are additional things that concern me. If you look at this instance, the fact that the members register does not record this so called transfer of the shares, the fact that the transfer occurred after the deemed date of liquidation which is unlawful anyway, the name of the company is wrong, the par value of the shares is incorrect. If the allegations contained in the liquidators affidavit is correct, this is not one of the most intellectual methods of trying to divest assets that I have ever seen Commentary nineteen Privately and publicy, Ben Ngubane is against the ropes. He says that as the matter pertaining to the Zululand Quarries is before a court he is not at liberty to comment. In November, the court will determine if the Ngubanes Zululand Querry share certificates are fraudulent. Meanwhile Eskom and the board leads, is running out of runway Pravin Gordhan In managing governance in South Africa where there are a significant number of people in the bureaucracy and elsewhere and the boards, who are actually taking a view that says I don’t care if you know what I do, I don’t care if you know that public resources are going elsewhere. I don’t care how many reports that the public protector or anybody else provides because I am protected. The question is by whom and at what cost and how will history record your role ultimately. THE END DURATION 10 36. PROMO ONE Chairperson of Eskom, Dr Ben Ngubane contends that his integrity is beyond reproach. This week MP’s grilled him on the Brian Molefe saga PROMO TWO In 2011, Dr Ben Ngubane and his wife bought Zululand Quarries through their company Huntrex 305. Court documents reveal that they have been accused of forging share certificates to lift the assets out of their liquidated company. PROMO THREE Did the Presidents attorney Michael Hulley, intervene in a matter between Dr Ben Ngubane and Ithala Bank who was owed millions by Ngubane’s company? metadata.Unique Selling Point: BEN NGUBANE AND HIS ZULULAND QUERRIES HUNTREX 305 Huntrex 305 is a company owned by Mr Ben Ngubane and his wife, that by itself is not unusual, but it’s the story of this company, that reveals much about the man installed as Eskom’s chairperson. Court documents reveal that Huntrex has defaulted on paying its loans, Ngubane has called upon his political connection, President Zuma to cover for him, and is now using the mining minister to delay court proceedings. Meanwhile court records reveal that he appears to have fraudulently forged false share certificates to hold onto a company that he hasn’t yet paid for. BEN NGUBANE BUYS A QARRY AND A SAND MINE The story begins in 2010 when Brikor, a brick company in Gauteng, ended up in a spot of financial bother. They were overdrawn on their overdraft facility by R30 million. FNB were unimpressed and wanted their money back. If not, they threatened Brikor that they would liquidate them. Brikor decided to free up some cash to repay FNB, by selling their STANGER operation for R50 million rand. The Stanger operation consisted of a sand mine and a quarry and the mineral rights for that. Enter willing buyers Mr Ben Ngubane and his wife Sheila. The Ngubane’s bought the entire operation and put it into what was a dormant company called Huntrex 305. Huntrex acquired all the assets of immovable property, the equipment and shares in Zululand quarries PTY LTD and Natal Sands PTY ltd. Presumably, they planned to operate the quarry and sand mining operation as a profitable business. It had a history of making a former rally driver very wealthy. Before Brikor owned the operation, it had been owned by rally driver called Jannie Habig, who had turned over R15 million rand a month and sold the business for R100 million to Brikor. NO MONEY HONEY But Ben Ngubane had no money to buy the business, so he approached the KZN provincial bank, Ithala for a loan of R30 million rand. The bank agreed. They funded the balance of R20 million in installments they would pay to Brikor who agreed to the terms, and the deal was sealed. THE HONEYMOON Now the Ngubane’s had themselves a quarry and sand mine, but with that came the repayments of the loan so they could call it their own. A million rand every month, R600 000 to Ithala bank and R400 000 to Brikor. For the first six months, they paid a million rand monthly, that they owed. Then after paying back less than 10% of the loan, they just stopped paying. ITHALA SAYS SHOW ME THE MONEY By the end of 2013 Ithala bank’s attorneys tell Ben and Sheila, that if they don’t pay up, the bank will liquidate Huntrex. The Ngubane’s responded by fighting back and bought an interdict to stop Ithala bank from liquidating them. In his application Ben Ngubane claimed that he had made a verbal arrangement with the CEO of Ithala bank that the loan wasn’t due and payable and therefore Ithala couldn’t liquidate! Ithala refuted this. TO COURT AND BACK AGAIN By Feb 2014 Ithala bank launched a counter application which included asking the court to provisionally liquidate the Ngubane’s company Huntrex. Its opposed. 2014 was spent backwards and forwards in a legal joust, until finally on the 31 March 2015 all the applications were set down to be heard. THE ESKOM CHAIRMAN, A CONVENIENT EXCUSE, AND AN UNWAVERING JUDGE Mr Ben Ngubane’s counsel stood up in court and told the judge that Mr Ngubane had been appointed as chairman of Eskom, he was busy with matters of national security and therefore the judge should postpone the matter indefinitely. But that didn’t wash with the judge, who said he didn’t care who the counsel’s client was, and without further ado he granted the provisional liquidation to ITHALA BANK. A FRONT POPS UP Four liquidators were appointed to manage Huntrex and keep the quarry going. One of the liquidators is an attorney at Stowell and Co. Attorneys, Mr Neil Button. “Our job was to preserve the assets” he told Carte Blanche. To ensure the business remained viable both Brikor and Ithala helped with some funding. The return date to put the company into final liquidation had been set down for August 2015, but the day before they were supposed to return to court, a lady called Janakey Reddy brought an application to put the company in Business rescue. She said she had sufficient funds to make it viable. But it turned out that Ms. Reddy was just the human resources manager at Huntrex ,who earned around R13 000 per month and had no other funding. She had been set up as a front by the NGUBANE’S. On the 10th December 2015, the court finally heard the two applications. The first was the case for business rescue which was defeated with costs, which is unfortunate for Mrs. Reddy as it meant she had to find the cost of several very expensive senior counsel. Then the liquidators fired her. MICHAEL HULLEY SWOOPS IN LIKE BEN NGUBANE’S ANGEL The second application heard on the 10th December was to confirm a date for final liquidation. Then counsel for Ithala bank makes a surprise admission. They tell the court that on the 9th December 2015, the day before they appeared in court, President Zuma’s attorney, Mr Michael Hulley, had arrived at ITHALA, convened a full board meeting of senior executives, and told them that the president had said they must “leave his man alone.” Ithala said no. Soon after Huntrex was put into final liquidation and Mr Hulley began to play a more prominent role. Mr Ngubanes original lawyer Mr Manogh Maharaj disappears. THE HOME STRETCH As per final liquidations, a process unfolds and a first meeting was held with creditors. The debts are discussed and by now they have ballooned to R75 million including interest: As at December 2015 HUNTREX owes: R34 million is owed to Ithala Bank R24 million to Brikor R1 million to the municipality in unpaid debts R4 million to the receiver for VAT R12 million to concurrent creditors Sandton Plant hire are keen buyers but they want to buy the whole bundle, the quarry, the sand mine, the mineral rights and the shares in Huntrex. But there’s a problem. Even though the shares in Huntrex have no value at that point, Ben Ngubane and Sheila are still shareholders. The liquidators put together a tripartite agreement and Mr Michael Hulley meets on Mr Ben Ngubane’s behalf. Meetings take place over the first six months of 2016 with Mr Hulley meeting the liquidators on behalf of Mr Ngubane who was away first in Brazil, then Nigeria, then the USA. Mr Hulley says in principle, Mr Ngubane will sell his shares. THE HOME STRETCH HITS A SNAG On the 15th June 2016 at the second meeting of the creditors it appears they are making progress. The liquidators have it recorded that they have received an offer of R30 million and Sheila Ngubane and her accountant adopts the report and sign the minutes. So far so good. But then suddenly Ben and Sheila produce another set of share certificate copies made out in their personal capacities. Ben Ngubane now refuses to sell his shares to the new buyer. THE MYSTERY OF ZULULAND QUERRIES The liquidators have both sets of share certificate and it appears the NGUBANE share certificates have been forged. The numbers are not consecutive as they should be; Zululand Quarries is spelt incorrectly as Zululand Querries, and instead of the shares being R1 each as they are in the originals they are recorded at one cent each. The shares should add up to 100 but instead one of the certificates has an adding mistake and reads 170 shares. Everyone is dumbstruck. Forging share certificates is a criminal offence under the companies act. Michael Hulley suddenly disappears from the scene and Mr Ngubane’s original lawyer Mr Maharaj enters the fray again. The liquidators ask the court for a declaratory order on the certificates but the Ngubanes oppose the declaratory order. MINISTER OF MINERAL AFFAIRS – GUPTA LINKED, MOSEBENZE ZWANE TO THE RESCUE. Currently there is an impasse. When the company was sold to the Ngubane’s the mineral rights changed hands without any problem. Strictly speaking, he should have had to reapply for a mining license due to the change of ownership. That didn’t happen, but now that the liquidators are trying to sell the business, the mining minister has intervened and said the new buyers must reapply for a mining right. The mining minister was supposed to file his affidavit by Tuesday this week. And that is where our story stands at present. Ngubane may yet hold onto an asset he has barely paid for, using the might of his political connections and the odd allegedly fraudulent share certificate.
